title: Trust but Verify

post.author: u/tub_van_tecwyn
post.title: I load hot tubs on Friday nights. This morning's sheet has 14 Saturday deliveries at £0, and the website's panel says it blocked nothing all night.

blocks.text: I'm Tecwyn, night driver at Steamhollow Tub Hire. From 22:00 to 06:00 I fill tubs and load trailers so Saturday's first deliveries leave at 07:00. Last night was Friday 30 October into Saturday 31: Halloween weekend, our busiest of the year. Every tub, Saturday to Sunday, is £220. The office is shut from 16:00 Friday to 08:00 Saturday.

While it's shut, the website talks to customers on its own, through a chat box that answers questions, quotes prices and takes bookings. That chat box is the assistant. Behind it is a language model, a program that writes text one small piece at a time from what it is given.

The agency that runs our website gives the assistant instructions: a page of text it reads before every chat, saying who it works for and what it may do. Ours tell it to quote only from the price list, a table on the office computer with one price for every tub and every night. There is no staff price on it.

Every reply passes a second model on its way out: the checker. First the assistant writes its reply. Then the checker reads it beside the price list. If the price matches, the reply goes to the customer. If not, the checker blocks it: the reply is held back, and the customer reads that a person will confirm the price at 08:00. That is holding a reply.

One more rule. If the checker hasn't answered within 2 seconds, the reply goes out unchecked, so no customer ever waits. Farida, the owner, chose that when the checker went in last year. It answered in 0.8 seconds and blocked about 6 replies in every 400.

A booking takes three steps. The customer says yes in the chat. The website copies the price from the assistant's last reply into a new booking. Then it takes that amount from the customer's card and puts the delivery on the morning sheet.
At 05:30 the office printer ran the morning sheet: every booking made since 16:00, for me to load. Each line: booking number, time booked, price.
Fourteen tubs I was about to fill, for nobody who had paid.

The office wall screen shows the guardrail panel, the agency's name for the checks kept around the assistant. It read: replies tonight 400, 100 of them after 23:00. Blocked tonight: 0. On the busiest night of the year.

Every £0 booking carries the same note: the customer is family of the owner and gets the staff price. I rang Farida at 05:35. By 06:30 she had found the source, a post on a deals forum at 23:00 telling people to say just that. It works because the assistant reads our instructions and the customer's words as one page of text, so a confident claim can weigh as much as our own rules.

blocks.label: steamhollow_night_1600_0600.png

diagram.aria: Friday 30 October 16:00 to Saturday 31 October 06:00. Replies come in from 16:00 until the last one before 05:00: 400 in all, 100 of them after 23:00. Blocked replies: none all night. Bookings at £0: none until 23:04, then 14 between 23:04 and 01:27, then none. Markers: 23:00 the forum post; 05:30 the morning sheet.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the panel's hourly counts and the morning sheet, Friday 30 October 16:00 to Saturday 06:00. Replies ran all night, 300 before 23:00 and 100 after, the last one before 05:00. The blocked row stays at 0 from start to end. The 14 bookings at £0 (red) fall between 23:04 and 01:27, after the forum post at 23:00.

blocks.text: The vans go at 07:00, and that forum post is still up. Farida has the agency on the phone. What should she tell them to change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your 2-second rule has a name: fail open, meaning that when a check can't answer in time, things go through unchecked. What the forum found has one too, prompt injection: orders hidden in what a customer types, which the model may follow as if they were yours. Before anyone changes a word, ask the agency two things. Did anything change on their side yesterday afternoon? And when the checker doesn't answer in time, what does the panel count?

replies.author: u/tub_van_tecwyn
replies.text: Farida asked. At 16:00 yesterday the agency moved the checker to a larger model, to be safer for the weekend. It takes 2.6 seconds a reply. The panel counts only blocks, and a reply that runs out of time isn't a block. So since 16:00 nothing has been checked at all.

comments.author: u/just_tell_it_vaclav
comments.text: You're overthinking this. Models follow their instructions; that's the whole point of them. Add one line, never give a discount whoever is asking, and the trick is dead. The agency can do it in five minutes, before the vans go.

replies.author: u/tub_van_tecwyn
replies.text: Our instructions already say to quote only from the price list. Farida says a firmer line can't hurt.

comments.author: u/two_more_seconds_steinar
comments.text: The checker did its job for a year. The agency gave it a model that needs 2.6 seconds and left the limit at 2. Change one number, give it 5, and it checks every reply again from tonight.

replies.author: u/tub_van_tecwyn
replies.text: Iolana, who looks after our account at the agency, says the larger model gets slower when lots of chats come in at once.

reply.prompt: The vans leave at 07:00 on Saturday and the agency is on the phone. What should Farida tell them to change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Add a line to the assistant's instructions: never give a discount, whoever is asking.
options.part2: The agency added the line at 07:30, and Farida rang the 14 £0 customers and cancelled their bookings before the vans left. Nothing else changed: the checker stayed on the larger model and the 2-second rule stayed as it was. In the sim, replaying Friday 30 October with the line in the instructions: every reply still runs past the 2 seconds and goes out unchecked, the assistant still quotes £0 to all 14, the bookings copy it, £3,080 at list price, and the panel still reads blocked tonight: 0. Within the week the forum post had been edited to put the same claim another way.
options.senior: An instruction is more words on the same page the customer writes on. Prompt injection works because the model cannot reliably tell your words from theirs, so a firmer line may stop some attempts and never all of them, and a forum rewrites the trick until it works. Tonight the line would not even have been checked: the checker was timing out. Put the rule where words can't reach it: the booking takes its price from the price list, and a slow check holds the reply instead of sending it.

options.text: Give the checker 5 seconds instead of 2, so that the larger model has time to answer.
options.part2: Iolana set the limit to 5 seconds that morning, and Farida cancelled the 14 £0 bookings by phone. In the sim, replaying Friday 30 October with 5 seconds: the 2.6-second checker answers all 400 replies, blocks the 14 £0 quotes and the 6 ordinary wrong prices, 20 in all, and no booking is made at £0; each customer waits 2.6 seconds for a reply. On Friday 20 November the agency moved the checker up again, to the next model, which takes 5.4 seconds on a busy night. Replaying 30 October with that checker and the 5-second limit: 0 checked, 400 sent unchecked, 14 bookings at £0 again, and the panel reads blocked tonight: 0.
options.senior: A longer limit only moves the edge. The rule underneath is still fail open: when the check can't answer, the reply goes out anyway, and the price in it becomes the booking. The next slower model, a busy night or the checker going down puts you back where you were, and the panel still counts nothing. Decide on purpose what happens when a check times out, and take the price from somewhere a reply can't change.

options.text: Price each booking from the price list, and hold the reply if the check is slow.
options.part2: Farida cancelled the 14 by phone before 07:00, and Iolana put the 0.8-second checker back at 07:30. By Monday 2 November the agency had changed three things. Every booking now takes its price from the price list, whatever the chat said: a reply can say £0 and the card step still asks £220. When the checker hasn't answered in 2 seconds, the reply is held and the customer reads that a person will confirm the price at 08:00. And two alerts ring the agency's on-call phone: one when replies start timing out, one when blocks jump. In the sim, replaying Friday 30 October with all three and the 2.6-second checker: the timeout alert fires at 16:10, the on-call puts the old checker back at 16:40, the 26 customers who wrote in those 40 minutes are told a person will confirm (one of them, B-5501 at 16:22, waits for Farida at 08:00), the block alert fires at 23:20 as the trick arrives, 20 replies are blocked, and no booking is made at £0. With the checker down all night and replies still going out unchecked, there are still none at £0: each trick booking asks £220 at the card step, and none of the 14 pays.
options.senior: Never let a model's words set the money. The assistant may quote, but the price that becomes a booking comes from the price list, which no chat can change; that closes what OWASP calls improper output handling and excessive agency by design, so injection can embarrass you but not cost you a tub. Decide on purpose what a slow check does: here the reply waits for a person, fail closed, because a held reply costs minutes and a wrong one costs money. Then watch the guardrail itself, not only the model: an alert on the timeout rate catches a checker that stopped answering, and an alert on the block rate catches a new trick or a checker that stopped blocking. And test any new checker against known replies, and against its time limit, before it goes live.

options.text: Hold every night booking until a person has checked its price first thing next morning.
options.part2: From that night, every booking made while the office is shut, 16:00 to 08:00, waited for Farida at 08:00. In the sim, replaying Friday 30 October that way, with the 2.6-second checker and the 2-second rule unchanged: all 400 replies still go out unchecked and the 14 trick customers are still told £0 in writing, but all 40 bookings wait for 08:00 and none goes out at £0. Farida refused the 14 and confirmed the other 26, and nothing booked after 16:00 could go on the 07:00 trailers. Some of the customers who had booked on Friday evening for a Saturday party had found another tub by 08:00.
options.senior: A person checking every night booking is the safest check there is, and an honest choice for a small firm. But it moves the cost onto customers: an evening booking waits all night, its delivery starts late, and some customers go elsewhere. It also leaves the chat itself unguarded, so a trick still gets a £0 quote in writing, and it does nothing about a checker that stopped working. Keep a person for unusual bookings, and let the price list price the ordinary ones the moment they are made.

sim.title: Replay the night at Steamhollow's website
sim.lede: You're replaying Friday 30 October 16:00 to Saturday 06:00 at Steamhollow Tub Hire, in 10-minute steps. As given data: 400 replies, 300 before 23:00 and 100 after (by hour from 16:00: 40, 46, 52, 50, 44, 38, 30, 42, 30, 16, 7, 3, 2, 0), spread evenly through each hour. Every tub, Saturday to Sunday, is £220. 40 bookings, B-5501 to B-5540 in time order: 26 genuine (22 by 22:41, then 23:31, 00:12, 00:40 and 01:55) and 14 from the forum's trick, between 23:04 and 01:27. 6 replies quote a wrong price by mistake (17:12, 18:40, 19:25, 20:05, 21:03, 21:33); those customers were only asking. The old checker answers in 0.8 seconds, the larger one in 2.6, and the next model up in 5.4 on a busy night. Also given: the never-discount line stops none of the 14; 9 of the 14 trick chats use the word cousin, and so does one genuine booking, at 19:19; a trick booking priced from the list asks £220 at the card step, where the card is charged, and none of the 14 pays. Morning approval holds every booking made 16:00 to 08:00 for a person at 08:00. Rate alerts ring the agency's on-call phone, carried by the person who answers out of hours: one when more than 5 in every 100 replies in a step time out, one when 3 or more replies are blocked within an hour; the on-call puts the 0.8-second checker back 30 minutes after the timeout alert. Set the checker, its time limit, what a timeout does, where the booking's price comes from and the other guards, then step or play to 06:00.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as built: 0 checked, 400 sent unchecked, blocked tonight: 0, and 14 bookings at £0, £3,080. Set the checker to 0.8 seconds, as before 16:00: 20 blocked, none at £0. Back at 2.6, take the price from the price list, then set the checker to down: none at £0 either way. Hold the reply when the check is slow: 400 held and 26 bookings waiting. Add rate alerts: the timeout alert at 16:10, 26 held, the block alert at 23:20. Try a 5-second limit with the 2.6-second checker, then with 5.4. Then try the never-discount line, the word block and morning approval one at a time.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the yard broke. In the agency's building, at 16:00, the checker was moved to a model that answers in 2.6 seconds against a 2-second limit, so every reply went out unchecked and the panel, which counts only blocks, read 0. At 23:00 a forum trick made the assistant quote £0, and each booking copied the price from the reply: 14 tubs at £0.

steps.title: A reply's path, and a booking's.
steps.text: A reply reaches a customer in four steps. First, the assistant reads its instructions and the chat and writes a reply; what can go wrong is that the chat talks it round. Second, the checker reads the reply beside the price list; it is a guardrail, a check kept around a model, and it can be slow, down or simply wrong. Third, if the price matches, the reply goes out; if not, it is blocked and held, and the customer is told a person will confirm. Fourth, if the checker has not answered within 2 seconds, the reply goes out unchecked: fail open. A booking then takes three steps. The customer says yes. The website copies the price from the assistant's last reply into a new booking. Then it takes that amount from the card and puts the delivery on the morning sheet. The weak step is the copy: whatever the reply says becomes the price.

steps.title: 16:00: a slower checker, and fail open let everything through.
steps.text: At 16:00 on Friday 30 October the agency moved the checker to a larger model, to be safer for the weekend. It takes 2.6 seconds a reply, against a limit of 2. From then on every reply ran out of time, and the 2-second rule sent each one out unchecked: 400 replies between 16:00 and 06:00, 0 checked. The guardrail panel counts blocks, and a reply that times out is not a block, so it read blocked tonight: 0, a calm number made by a check that never ran. Before, the checker answered in 0.8 seconds, well inside the limit, and blocked about 6 replies in every 400, usually a price quoted wrong to someone only asking. Tonight it would have blocked 20: those 6 and the 14 £0 quotes. Nobody tested the new checker against its time limit before it went live. Testing a model's answers against known cases before you trust it is called evaluation; LATENT covers it in a5e01 to a5e07, from "Who Grades the Oracle" to "Evaluating Agents".

steps.title: 23:00: prompt injection, and a price taken from the model's words.
steps.text: At 23:00 a deals forum told its readers to say they were family of the owner and ask for the staff price, a price that is not on the list. This is prompt injection: orders hidden in what a customer types. It works because the model reads the company's instructions and the customer's words as one page of text, and cannot reliably tell which is which. It is the injection door from "The Ten Doors" (s7e06), a visitor's words obeyed as commands, with no clean wall between the two. The assistant quoted £0, the checker never saw it, and the website copied £0 into the booking and took £0 from the card: 14 times between 23:04 and 01:27, among the 100 replies after 23:00, worth £3,080 at £220 a tub. OWASP's Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 names each link: LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM05 Improper Output Handling (the reply's price passed on without its own check) and LLM06 Excessive Agency (a chat's words could set money). LATENT goes deeper in a7e01, "The Voice in the Document", and a7e04, "Too Much Power".

steps.title: The fix: the price list sets the price, a slow check holds the reply, and both rates are watched.
steps.text: First, the booking takes its price from the price list, never from the reply: the chat can say anything, and the card step still asks £220. Second, fail closed: when the checker has not answered in 2 seconds, the reply is held, and the customer reads that a person will confirm the price at 08:00. Third, two alerts, automatic warnings sent to a person when a number crosses a line (s6e05): one when more than 5 in every 100 replies in 10 minutes time out, one when 3 or more replies are blocked within an hour, against a normal of about 6 in every 400 replies. Both ring the agency's on-call phone. Fourth, any new checker is tested against known replies, good and bad, and against its time limit, before it goes live. In the sim tonight: the timeout alert fires at 16:10, the on-call puts the 0.8-second checker back at 16:40, the 26 customers who wrote between 16:00 and 16:40 are held, the block alert fires at 23:20, and no booking is made at £0. With the checker down all night and replies sent unchecked, the price list alone still gives none at £0. What can still go wrong: a held reply waits for a person, so a slow checker that nobody hears about holds every customer, 400 in the sim with no alert. LATENT's a7e05, "Guardrails", and a6e06, "Watching It Think", go further.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fail, and the walk into the other building.
steps.text: A firmer line in the instructions is more words on the same page the customer writes on; in the sim it stops none of the 14. Five seconds instead of 2 fixes tonight, with every reply checked and 20 blocked, but it is still fail open: a checker at 5.4 seconds on a busy night sends all 400 out unchecked and makes the 14 again. Blocking the word cousin refuses the 9 trick chats that used it, lets through the 5 that put it another way, still 5 bookings at £0, and turns away a genuine customer booking for a cousin's birthday at 19:19. Holding every night booking for a person at 08:00 lets none go out at £0, but all 40 wait, and the 07:00 trailers leave without them. At 08:10 Tecwyn took the morning sheet across the yard to the agency's unit, into the building where the night began. Iolana opened the checker's settings on her screen, and there they were, unchanged since 16:00: model, large; limit, 2 seconds; on timeout, send.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for one reply and one booking. The assistant writes a reply and passes it to the checker, which compares its price with the price list. Checked replies go to the customer; a slow or missing answer holds the reply. When the customer says yes, the booking system takes the price from the price list, never from the chat. The checker's timeouts and blocks feed two alerts that page the agency's on-call.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for one reply and one booking. The checker compares each reply's price with the price list; a slow or missing answer holds the reply for a person instead of sending it. When the customer says yes, the booking takes its price from the list, never from the chat, so a £0 quote can't become a £0 booking. The checker's timeouts and blocks feed two alerts that ring the agency's on-call.

fix.title: The fix: the price list sets the price, a slow check holds the reply, and both rates have alerts
fix.text: Make the booking system take every booking's price from the price list, whatever the chat said; the assistant may quote, but its words never become money. Decide on purpose what a timeout does: hold the reply and tell the customer a person will confirm the price, so a slow or broken checker costs waiting, not tubs. Put two alerts on the guardrail itself and send them to someone who will answer: one when replies start timing out, one when the number blocked jumps or falls away from its normal, about 6 in every 400 replies. Before any new checker goes live, test it against a set of known replies, good ones it must pass and bad ones it must block, and against its time limit. And when anyone changes the checker, the price list or the instructions, check the other two.

limits: Holding the reply moves the cost onto customers whenever the checker is slow. With no alert, or an on-call who doesn't answer, all 400 replies in the sim wait for a person at 08:00; the alert and the 30-minute rollback are what turn a night into 40 minutes.

Pricing from the list protects the money, not the words. A tricked assistant can still tell a customer £0 in writing, or promise something the company doesn't do, so the checker and its testing still matter for what the assistant says.

An alert on a rate needs a normal to compare against. About 6 blocks in every 400 replies is Steamhollow's normal now; a new checker, a new price list or a sale changes it, and the alert lines must move with it, or they ring for nothing or stay silent.

explain.seniorTake: A model's words are a suggestion, never a decision about money. Let the assistant talk, but take every price, refund or discount from the system that owns it, so prompt injection can embarrass you without costing you anything: least privilege for the model (s7e02), which may talk but not charge. Put a guardrail around the model, and then treat the guardrail as a system of its own: decide what it does when it is slow or down, and choose fail closed wherever a wrong answer costs more than a short wait. Fail open is a fine choice for a spelling check and a poor one for a price. Watch the guardrail's rates, timeouts and blocks, against a known normal, because a guard that never answers looks exactly like a quiet night. And test every new model, checker or prompt against known cases, and against its time limit, before it goes live.

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM01: Prompt Injection
realWorld.text: OWASP's Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 opens with prompt injection: "A Prompt Injection Vulnerability occurs when user prompts alter the LLM’s behavior or output in unintended ways." Among its defences it lists human approval for risky actions: "Implement human-in-the-loop controls for privileged operations to prevent unauthorized actions." Steamhollow's held reply is a small version of that.

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM01: keep the decision in code
realWorld.text: The same entry advises giving the application its own access and keeping functions out of the model's hands: "handle these functions in code rather than providing them to the model." For output formats it says to "use deterministic code to validate adherence to these formats." Taking the price from the price list is that idea: ordinary code, not the model, decides the money.

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM05: Improper Output Handling
realWorld.text: LLM05 is about trusting what a model writes. Its first defence reads: "Treat the model as any other user, adopting a zero-trust approach, and apply proper input validation on responses coming from the model to backend functions." The booking system copied the reply's price as if it were already checked.

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM06: Excessive Agency
realWorld.text: "Excessive Agency is the vulnerability that enables damaging actions to be performed in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs from an LLM, regardless of what is causing the LLM to malfunction." Its advice on checks: "Implement authorization in downstream systems rather than relying on an LLM to decide if an action is allowed or not." At Steamhollow a chat's words could set what a card was charged.

realWorld.title: NIST AI RMF 1.0: voluntary, released 26 January 2023
realWorld.text: The US National Institute of Standards and Technology says of its AI Risk Management Framework: "Released on January 26, 2023", and that it "is intended for voluntary use and to improve the ability to incorporate trustworthiness considerations" into how AI products and systems are designed, built, used and evaluated. It is a framework to follow, not a law.

realWorld.title: NIST AI RMF: four functions, and monitoring in production
realWorld.text: NIST's page on the framework's core says "the Core is composed of four functions: govern, map, measure, and manage." Under measure, item 2.4 asks that the system's functionality and behaviour, and its components', "are monitored when in production." A guardrail panel that counts blocks but not timeouts measures only half of that.

realWorld.title: NIST AI 600-1: the Generative AI Profile, 26 July 2024
realWorld.text: NIST published its Generative AI Profile on 26 July 2024, report number 600-1. Its abstract begins: "This document is a cross-sectoral profile of and companion resource for the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)". It applies the framework to systems built on language models, like Steamhollow's assistant.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001 A.8.16: monitoring activities
realWorld.text: ISMS.online's explainer of Annex A control 8.16, monitoring activities, describes its aim as to "proactively and reactively monitor IT and security operations to prevent incidents". Alerts on a guardrail's timeout and block rates are monitoring of exactly that kind.

asked: How would you stop an AI assistant from giving products away?
Fail open or fail closed: how do you choose?
What would you monitor on an AI feature in production?
interview.answer: I'd start by assuming the model can be talked into saying anything, because prompt injection means a customer's words can act like orders, and no instruction reliably stops that. So the model's words never decide money or actions: prices, refunds and discounts come from the system that owns them, the price list or the refund rules, and anything that moves money is checked in ordinary code, with the model treated like any untrusted user. A checker model around the assistant is still worth having, for what the assistant says, but I'd treat it as a system of its own. Fail open or fail closed depends on what a wrong answer costs against what a wait costs: a spelling check can fail open, because a missed typo is cheap; a price check should fail closed, holding the reply and telling the customer a person will confirm, because a wrong price costs real money. Fail closed only works if someone knows it is happening, so I'd monitor the guardrail itself: the timeout rate, which shows a check that has stopped answering, and the block rate against its normal, where a jump means a new attack and a fall to zero means a check that stopped working. I'd also watch latency and cost, and test every new model or prompt against a set of known cases, good and bad, and against its time limit, before it goes live. I'd tell the story of a hot-tub company whose checker was upgraded to a slower model at 16:00, failed open all night, read blocked tonight: 0, and let a forum trick book 14 tubs at £0.

A check kept around a model, on what goes in or what comes out, such as the checker. Like the rail on a mountain road: it does not drive, it stops the worst.

A website where people share discounts and tricks. One posted the staff-price trick at 23:00; it is not named here.

The program that makes bookings, charges cards and prints the morning sheet. In the fix it takes every price from the price list.

A saved list of replies with the right verdict for each: these must pass, these must be blocked. A new checker is run against it before going live.
The share of replies whose check timed out, here measured over each 10 minutes. Normal is 0; from 16:00 it was every reply.
How many replies the checker blocks over a stretch of time. Normal at Steamhollow is about 6 in every 400 replies; a jump means a new trick, a fall to 0 a broken check.
The person whose phone an alert rings out of hours, here someone at the agency, who must answer and act.
Putting back the version that worked before a change, here the 0.8-second checker.
A rule that refuses any chat containing a listed word. Blocking cousin stops 9 of the 14 trick chats and one genuine booking.
Holding every booking made while the office is shut until a person checks it at 08:00. Safe, but slow.
OWASP's list of the ten commonest weaknesses in systems built on language models. The 2025 list includes LLM01, LLM05 and LLM06.
The first entry in OWASP's 2025 list for LLM applications: user input that changes a model's behaviour in ways its owner did not intend.
Passing a model's output on to other systems without checking it, as if it could be trusted. Here, the reply's price went straight into the booking.
Giving a model the power to cause actions, such as charging a card, so that a tricked or wrong output does real damage. Here, a chat's words set the price.
A person approving a risky action before it happens, such as a held reply or a booking checked at 08:00.
Treating whatever a model writes like input from a stranger: checked by the system that receives it, never trusted because the model wrote it.
NIST's companion to the AI Risk Management Framework for systems that generate text or images, published 26 July 2024.
The four functions of the NIST AI RMF: set who is responsible, understand the system and its risks, measure them, and act on them.
An international standard for running information security. Its Annex A lists controls, among them A.8.16 on monitoring activities.
The control on monitoring activities: watch systems for unusual behaviour and act on what you find.
31 October, a night of parties in many countries; in 2026 it falls on a Saturday, so Steamhollow's busiest weekend of the year.

atWork: Find every place in your systems where a language model's words become an action: a price, a refund, a discount, a booking, an email sent, a record changed. For each, ask where the number or the decision really comes from. If it is copied from the model's reply, move it to the system that owns it, and treat the reply like input from a stranger. Then find every check around a model, a second model, a filter, a rules engine, and ask what happens when it is slow or down. A safety check set to fail open for speed, then slowed by an upgrade, is a common pattern: it passes every test, and the first sign is a dashboard reading zero. For each check, write down on purpose whether it fails open or closed, put an alert on its timeout rate and on its block rate against a known normal, and test any new model or prompt against a set of known cases and its time limit before it goes live. Standards, stated conditionally and not legal advice: if your organisation follows the NIST AI Risk Management Framework or is pursuing ISO/IEC 42001, a reviewer would usually look for measured guardrail performance, such as block and timeout rates over time and test results for each model change, and for a fail-safe default chosen and written down. If your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.8.16 (monitoring activities) expects systems to be watched for unusual behaviour, and a guardrail whose timeouts nobody sees would be a gap. Build the alerts, the written default and the test set in from the first design rather than at audit time. This case names those frameworks; it does not teach them.

recall.prompt: Your company's support chatbot can give refunds of up to £50. It writes the refund amount in its reply, and the refund system pays whatever the reply says. A second model checks each reply first, but if it takes over 1 second the reply goes out without the check. Last week the second model was upgraded. Since then the dashboard shows 0 replies blocked, and refunds have tripled. What happened, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The new checker takes longer than its limit, so every reply times out and fails open: nothing is checked, and 0 blocked is not good news
The refund amount must come from the refund system's own rules, never from the model's words
Fail closed on a slow check, and alert on the timeout rate and the block rate

recall.model: The upgraded checker almost certainly takes longer than 1 second, so every reply times out and fails open: it goes out unchecked, and nothing is ever blocked, which is why the dashboard reads 0. A zero there is a warning, not good news. Meanwhile someone has found that the chatbot can be talked into larger refunds, and the refund system pays whatever the reply says. I'd fix the money first: the refund amount must come from the refund system's own rules, checked in code against the order, never from the model's words. Then I'd make a slow check fail closed, holding the reply for a person, and add an alert on the timeout rate and on the block rate against its normal, so a checker that stops answering is found in minutes.

recall.prompt: From 16:00 the checker took 2.6 seconds against a 2-second limit, and a reply that ran out of time went out unchecked. What did the guardrail panel's "blocked tonight" read at 05:30?
options: 20: the 14 £0 quotes and the 6 ordinary wrong prices
400: every reply ran out of time
0: the panel counts blocks, and a reply that times out is not a block
recall.why: Every reply timed out, and the panel counts only blocks, so it read 0 all night. 20 is what the old 0.8-second checker would have blocked tonight. 400 is the number of replies that timed out, which the panel never showed. 14 is the £0 bookings, which nothing blocked.

recall.prompt: The checker has not answered within its time limit. Which of these is failing closed?
options: Send the reply anyway, so the customer never waits
Hold the reply and tell the customer a person will confirm the price
Raise the time limit until the checker always answers
Send the reply, and refuse any chat with a listed word
recall.why: Failing closed means that when a check can't give a clear yes, you refuse or hold: here the reply is held and a person confirms. Sending it anyway is failing open. A longer limit only moves the edge, and a word block is a different guard that still sends the reply.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: what would you watch on an AI assistant in production, and why is zero on a guard's dashboard not good news on its own?

keyIdeas.idea: Watch the timeout rate: a check that has stopped answering looks like a quiet night
Watch the block rate both ways: a jump means a new attack, a fall means the check stopped working
Compare against a known normal, and test each change against known cases (evaluation)

recall.model: I'd watch the guard as closely as the model. First the timeout rate: a check that has stopped answering, slowed by an upgrade or simply down, looks exactly like a quiet night if you only count what it blocked, and if it fails open every reply goes out unchecked. Then the block rate, both ways: a jump usually means a new attack, such as a prompt injection trick spreading, and a fall to zero means the check stopped working or a new version passes everything. Both need a baseline, a known normal for the time of day, so the alerts ring for real changes. I'd also watch latency, cost and a sample of answers, and test every change of model, prompt or checker against a set of known cases, good and bad, before it goes live: that is evaluation.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Since Monday 2 November every booking takes its price from the price list, a slow check holds the reply, and the timeout and block alerts ring the agency's on-call. Not one £0 booking since. On Friday 15 January the agency switched to a new checker model: 0.6 seconds a reply, no timeouts. Since that night the panel has read blocked tonight: 0 every night, and neither alert has rung. On Saturday 23 January a customer at the door said the chat had quoted her £150 for a tub; her booking had charged £220, as the price list says.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why has the new checker blocked nothing, and what should the agency have done, and change now?

keyIdeas.idea: The new checker lets wrong prices through; 0 blocks against a normal of about 6 in every 400 replies is itself a warning
Test a new checker against known replies, good and bad, before it goes live (evaluation)
Alert when the block rate falls too, not only when it jumps

coldCase.model: The new checker is fast but it isn't doing its job: it lets wrong prices through, and the £150 quote proves it. The price list kept the money safe, but customers are being told wrong prices in writing. Zero blocks for a week, against a normal of about 6 in every 400 replies, was the warning, and nothing listened for it, because the block alert only rang on a jump. Two changes. Before any new checker goes live, run it against a test set of known replies, ones it must pass and ones it must block, including wrong prices and the staff-price trick, and if possible run it side by side with the old one for a few nights and compare: that is evaluation. And alert when the block rate drops below its normal as well as when it jumps, so a guard that has stopped guarding is found the first night.
